extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and reporters who cover police, municipal, criminal and civil courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about police, municipal, criminal and civil court proceedings — what facts to gather and how to present them (testimony, outcomes, background, human detail, Q&A examples). Uses sample court stories to illustrate technique and required elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important testimony
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the key testimony given in court — who said what and the substance of their statements. Use witness accounts and relevant quotes (e.g., confessions, admissions, explanatory narratives) to convey the heart of the case; when necessary use interpreters and note that testimony may change the complexion of a case (see Chinese girls' statements and the forgery confession).

rubrics_metrics.name: Net results of the day's proceedings in a trial
rubrics_metrics.description: net results of the day's proceedings in a trial
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the immediate outcomes of the day's session: verdicts, motions, adjournments, continuances, bail decisions, fines remitted, or other dispositions. Give concrete figures and follow-up dates (examples: fines remitted; bail set at $300; cases adjourned for further hearing).

rubrics_metrics.name: The history of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.description: the history of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background and prior history relevant to the present proceeding — prior arrests, previous suits, past convictions, and sequence of events leading up to current charges (e.g., chronic schemes described in the grand larceny and counterfeiting stories). This helps readers understand context and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions of a will
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting estate or probate matters, state specific provisions of the will that are at issue (who receives what, special bequests, contested clauses). The book lists this as an essential item to include in such coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bankruptcy reporting, include the creditor/debtor liabilities, the assets involved, and the cause or reason for bankruptcy. These financial particulars are core facts that inform readers about the dispute or proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: The award, or finding
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report any awards or judicial findings — verdicts, damages awarded, judgments, or official findings of fact. State amounts, terms, and who received them (court orders, jury awards, findings of liability or innocence).

rubrics_metrics.name: The grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.description: the grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out the legal basis or grounds for the action: the claims, causes of action, statutes or alleged wrongs relied upon by plaintiffs or the prosecution. Explain briefly why the suit was brought and the theory of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest details and scene description
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive narration and human details to make court stories vivid
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring courtroom scenes and parties to life with sensory detail, emotion and narrative: ages, small gestures, sobbing relatives, the look of the bench, children's demeanor, the prisoner's background, dwellings (e.g., the runaway boy's hut), and moral or human consequences. These elements engage readers and illustrate the human side of legal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report identifying details of persons and places
rubrics_metrics.description: Give names, addresses, ages, occupations and official titles
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify participants clearly — full names, street addresses, ages, occupations, institutional affiliations, and titles (judge, detective, attorney). The examples consistently supply such details (e.g., 'Chief John H. Monroe', addresses, ages of the girls), which lend precision and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: State charges, pleas and specific legal actions
rubrics_metrics.description: List charges, pleas entered, counts, and procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out the formal charges, the defendant's plea (guilty/not guilty), counts, any special statutory designations, and immediate procedural actions (binding over to trial, information to be filed). Include statutory penalties or maximum sentences when relevant (e.g., imprisonment not exceeding thirty days; penalty ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations and Q&A excerpts for testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce verbatim quotes and, where useful, Q&A exchanges from the courtroom
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct quotations for color and accuracy, and include short Q&A excerpts where the form of questioning illuminates the testimony (as in the Schepps Q&A). Quoted language can reveal demeanor, inconsistencies, or key admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey courtroom demeanor, conduct and reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how participants behave and how the courtroom reacts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note jurors' and judges' reactions, witness demeanor (nervousness, flippancy, bravado), attorneys' tactics, and the atmosphere (laughter, silence, tension). These observations add interpretive value and help readers grasp the tenor of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear chronology and specific times/dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out events in time order with dates and times where available
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When narrating incidents or testimony, present a clear timeline (dates, times, sequence of movements or actions). Detailed chronology aids reader comprehension of how events unfolded (examples: Wilson's step-by-step account of the theft and the times he traveled).
